opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people come at this question from the wrong direction. They look at the Transformer and they list its weaknesses: quadratic attention, fixed context windows, the way it struggles with certain kinds of long-horizon reasoning or continual learning, and they say, "Okay, we need something that fixes these." And that's a fine exercise, but if that's all you do, you tend to end up with architectures that are clever on paper and then lose at scale.

What I mean by appreciating how far they've carried us is really understanding *why* the Transformer won. It wasn't that it was the most expressive architecture anyone had ever proposed. It was that it was incredibly friendly to the hardware we had, it parallelized beautifully during training, it was simple enough that thousands of people could iterate on it, and it kept getting better as you poured more compute and data into it. That last property is the one people underrate. For almost a decade now, every time we scaled it up, it rewarded us. Pretraining, then instruction tuning, then RL on top of it for reasoning. The same basic block absorbed all of that.

So if you want to replace it, you have to clear a very high bar. You're not competing against the 2017 paper. You're competing against an enormous accumulated stack of engineering: kernels, optimizers, training recipes, inference systems, intuitions about hyperparameters, all of which have been tuned around this one architecture. A new idea that's ten percent better in a small-scale experiment can easily be worse in practice once you account for all of that.

And I think the humility part matters too. A lot of things we confidently said Transformers couldn't do, they ended up doing once we found the right training setup. So before you declare something a fundamental architectural limitation, you should be pretty sure it's not just a data or training-objective problem in disguise.

That said, I do think we'll eventually move past it. But the thing that replaces it will probably look like it learned the right lessons from the Transformer: scalability, simplicity, hardware alignment, rather than something that just tries to patch its weak spots.

r001.rationale: The response says that focusing only on Transformer weaknesses can produce ideas that lose at scale; it argues a replacement must also preserve the qualities that made Transformers successful.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare how often architecture research pursues efficiency versus greater expressive power.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a tendency, especially in research circles, to treat the Transformer as this thing we're all impatiently waiting to get rid of. Every few months there's a new architecture paper and the framing is always "this is what comes after attention." And I understand the impulse, because you look at quadratic attention cost, or the fact that the thing doesn't have a persistent state the way you'd intuitively want, and you think, surely we can do better than this.

But my view is that if you don't deeply understand why the Transformer won, you're going to keep proposing replacements that lose. And it won for reasons that are not accidental. It's almost embarrassingly simple to implement. It parallelizes beautifully during training, which is really the thing — you can throw an enormous amount of compute at it and the compute actually gets used. It's robust to a lot of hyperparameter sloppiness. And the scaling behavior is just extremely well-behaved, which means you can make predictions about what a bigger run will do before you spend the money. Those are not small properties. Those are the properties that let you go from a research curiosity to something that's actually changing how people work.

So when I say the first step to replacing it is appreciating how far it's carried us, I mean that pretty literally. The bar isn't "better on some benchmark at a small scale." The bar is: does it preserve all of those things — the simplicity, the hardware fit, the predictable scaling — and then add something on top? A lot of alternatives that look good at a few hundred million parameters quietly give up one of those, and then at scale the Transformer just catches up and passes them. We've seen that movie several times now.

And honestly, I think there's a kind of humility in it. The field didn't arrive at this architecture because it was elegant. It arrived there because it worked, and then kept working at every scale we tried. Whatever comes next has to earn its place the same way. I'd love to see it happen, I think it probably will happen, but I think the people who get there will be the ones who respect the thing they're trying to replace rather than the ones who are just tired of it.

r001.rationale: The response says replacements should preserve the Transformer’s strengths and add something, and mentions its weaknesses, but does not argue that alternatives failing to address those strengths should focus on those weaknesses.

r002.rationale: It notes attention cost and persistent state as concerns in architecture research, but does not say research favors making Transformers cheaper or more efficient over increasing expressive power.

astra-6.text:
I mean that before we look for the next architecture, we should understand what makes this one so successful. Transformers gave us a way to take a very general learning procedure, apply it to enormous amounts of data, and keep getting better results as we put more compute into it. That’s a remarkable foundation.

And when you’re trying to replace that foundation, you have to be honest about what you’re comparing against. It’s not enough to have a beautiful idea that wins on one small benchmark. Can you train it efficiently? Does it scale? Can it learn the range of things we want these systems to learn?

So appreciating Transformers isn’t saying they’re the final answer. It’s understanding which properties we need to preserve and where there’s actually room to improve. Otherwise, you can spend a lot of time replacing something without making it better.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a replacement should preserve Transformers’ successful properties and identify room to improve, but it does not state that an alternative that leaves their strengths unaddressed should focus specifically on Transformer weaknesses.

r002.rationale: It mentions training efficiency and scaling as evaluation criteria, but does not observe that architecture research tends to emphasize cost or efficiency over expressive power.

sol-6.1.text:
I mean that before we talk about what comes next, we should understand why Transformers have worked so well. They gave us an architecture that is flexible, that trains efficiently at scale, and that keeps improving as we put more compute and data into it. That’s an extraordinary foundation.

So if you want to replace them, you need more than an interesting architectural idea. You need to preserve what makes them successful while solving something they struggle with. Maybe that’s how efficiently they use context, how they maintain state, or how much computation they need to solve a problem. The question is: what limitation are we actually removing, and does the new architecture still work when we scale it?

Appreciating Transformers means setting the right bar for their successor.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a successor should preserve Transformers’ strengths while addressing something they struggle with, and asks which limitation the new architecture removes.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not compare how often architecture research targets lower cost or greater efficiency versus increased expressive power.
